P.title: P.blurb
Psychology: Biases, memory, habits, social influence and emotions.

P.title: ps-biases.summary
Psychology: The mental shortcuts that fool everyone.

P.title: ps-biases.q0.q
Psychology: A shop shows "was €300, now €120". Which bias makes it feel cheap?

P.title: ps-biases.q1.q
Psychology: Keeping a bad investment because of what you already paid is the…

P.title: ps-biases.q1.x
Psychology: Only future costs and benefits matter.

P.title: ps-biases.q2.q
Psychology: Roughly how much more does a loss hurt than an equal gain?

P.title: ps-biases.q2.x
Psychology: Loss aversion, measured by Kahneman and Tversky.

P.title: ps-biases.c0.text
Psychology: Psychologist Daniel Kahneman described two modes of thinking. System 1 is fast, automatic and intuitive. System 2 is slow, effortful and logical. Most biases come from System 1 answering before System 2 checks.

P.title: ps-biases.c1.text
Psychology: We notice, remember and trust information that agrees with what we already believe, and dismiss what doesn't. It's why two people can read the same news and both feel proven right.

P.title: ps-biases.c2.text
Psychology: The first number you hear pulls your estimate towards it, even if it's random. A jacket "reduced from €300 to €120" feels cheap because €300 became the anchor.

P.title: ps-biases.c3.text
Psychology: We judge how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind. Plane crashes make the news, so flying feels riskier than driving, though per kilometre it's far safer.

P.title: ps-biases.c4.text
Psychology: We keep investing in something because of what we've already spent, not because of what's to come. Finishing a bad film because you paid for the ticket is a classic case.

P.title: ps-biases.c4.viz.items.0.r
Psychology: Is it worth it from now on?

P.title: ps-biases.c5.text
Psychology: Losing €50 hurts roughly twice as much as winning €50 feels good. That's why people take big risks to avoid a loss but play safe to protect a gain.

P.title: ps-biases.c6.text
Psychology: People with a little knowledge often overrate their skill, because they don't yet know what they don't know. As expertise grows, confidence first dips, then rises with real skill.

P.title: ps-biases.c7.text
Psychology: We study the winners and forget the failures we can't see. "Drop out of university like the famous founders" ignores the thousands who dropped out and didn't succeed.

P.title: ps-biases.c8.text
Psychology: The same fact feels different depending on the wording. Patients choose a surgery with a "90% survival rate" far more often than one with a "10% death rate", though they're identical.

P.title: ps-biases.c9.text
Psychology: You can't switch biases off, but you can slow down for important choices: look for opposing evidence, ask "what would change my mind?", and decide before you see the anchor.

P.title: ps-biases.c9.viz.items.1
Psychology: Ask what would change your mind

P.title: ps-biases.c9.viz.items.2
Psychology: Set your budget before seeing prices

P.title: ps-memory.summary
Psychology: Why you forget, and how to remember better.

P.title: ps-memory.q0.q
Psychology: Which study method strengthens memory most?

P.title: ps-memory.q2.q
Psychology: Why is an all-nighter bad before an exam?

P.title: ps-memory.q2.x
Psychology: Deep sleep moves learning into long-term memory.

P.title: ps-memory.c0.text
Psychology: Memory has three stages: encoding (taking information in), storage (keeping it) and retrieval (getting it back). Most "forgetting" is actually a failure to encode or retrieve.

P.title: ps-memory.c1.text
Psychology: Working memory holds only a few items for seconds, about 4 chunks. Long-term memory has practically no limit and can last a lifetime.

P.title: ps-memory.c2.text
Psychology: Hermann Ebbinghaus showed in 1885 that we forget fast: much of new material is gone within a day unless we review it. Each review flattens the curve.

P.title: ps-memory.c3.text
Psychology: Reviewing just before you'd forget is the most efficient way to learn. Intervals grow each time: 1 day, 3 days, a week, a month. This app's review queue uses the same idea.

P.title: ps-memory.c4.text
Psychology: Testing yourself beats rereading. Trying to pull an answer out of memory strengthens it far more than looking at it again, even when you get it wrong.

P.title: ps-memory.c5.text
Psychology: We remember more by grouping items into meaningful chunks. A phone number like 912345678 is easier as 912 345 678, and chess masters see board patterns, not single pieces.

P.title: ps-memory.c6.text
Psychology: During deep sleep the brain replays the day's experiences and moves them into long-term storage. Pulling an all-nighter before an exam hurts the very memories you need.

P.title: ps-memory.c7.text
Psychology: Memories are rebuilt every time we recall them, so they can change. Elizabeth Loftus showed that a leading question ("how fast were the cars when they smashed?") alters what witnesses remember.

P.title: ps-memory.c8.text
Psychology: An ancient technique: imagine a familiar place and put each item to remember at a spot along a route. Walking the route in your mind brings the items back. Memory champions use it.

P.title: ps-memory.c9.text
Psychology: Combine the tricks: short sessions, test yourself, space the reviews and sleep. Ten minutes a day with this app beats two hours once a week.

P.title: ps-motivation.summary
Psychology: Why we do what we do, and how to change it.

P.title: ps-motivation.q0.q
Psychology: What are the three parts of the habit loop?

P.title: ps-motivation.q1.x
Psychology: Too easy is boring; too hard causes anxiety.

P.title: ps-motivation.c0.text
Psychology: Habits run on a loop: a cue triggers a routine, which brings a reward. Over time the brain links the cue to the reward and runs the routine automatically.

P.title: ps-motivation.c1.text
Psychology: Small friction changes behaviour a lot. Put the fruit on the counter and the biscuits in a high cupboard; lay out your running shoes the night before.

P.title: ps-motivation.c2.text
Psychology: Start absurdly small: one push-up, one page, two minutes. Small wins build identity ("I'm someone who exercises"), and it's easier to grow a habit than to start one.

P.title: ps-motivation.c3.text
Psychology: Attach a new habit to an existing one: "After I pour my morning coffee, I'll write three lines in my journal." The old habit becomes the cue.

P.title: ps-motivation.c4.text
Psychology: Intrinsic motivation comes from enjoying the thing itself; extrinsic from rewards or pressure. Paying people for something they already enjoy can sometimes reduce their interest.

P.title: ps-motivation.c5.text
Psychology: Psychologists Deci and Ryan found three needs that fuel lasting motivation: autonomy (choice), competence (getting better) and relatedness (connection with others).

P.title: ps-motivation.c6.text
Psychology: Dopamine is less about pleasure and more about wanting and anticipation. It spikes when we expect a reward, which is why notifications and endless feeds are so gripping.

P.title: ps-motivation.c7.text
Psychology: In the famous "marshmallow test", children could eat one treat now or wait for two. Later studies suggest family background and trust explain much of who waits.

P.title: ps-motivation.c8.text
Psychology: Flow is the state of total absorption, when time disappears. Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi found it happens when a challenge matches your skill, neither too easy nor too hard.

P.title: ps-motivation.c9.text
Psychology: Cue: after dinner. Routine: read one page on the sofa, phone in another room. Reward: tick it on a calendar. Two months later, it's automatic.

P.title: ps-social.summary
Psychology: How other people change what we think and do.

P.title: ps-social.q0.q
Psychology: Why do crowds sometimes fail to help in an emergency?

P.title: ps-social.q1.q
Psychology: Long queues outside a restaurant persuade us through…

P.title: ps-social.q1.x
Psychology: We assume many people can't be wrong.

P.title: ps-social.c0.text
Psychology: In Solomon Asch's 1950s experiments, people judged which line matched another. When actors all gave the wrong answer, many participants went along at least once.

P.title: ps-social.c1.text
Psychology: Stanley Milgram's 1960s experiment found many ordinary people would give what they believed were dangerous electric shocks when an authority figure told them to continue. No shocks were real.

P.title: ps-social.c2.text
Psychology: The more people who witness an emergency, the less likely any one of them is to help: each assumes someone else will. Pointing at one person, "you, call 112!", breaks the spell.

P.title: ps-social.c2.viz.items.0.r
Psychology: You in the red jacket, call 112!

P.title: ps-social.c3.text
Psychology: When unsure, we copy others. Reviews, queues outside restaurants and "best-seller" labels all work because we assume many people can't be wrong.

P.title: ps-social.c4.text
Psychology: One good trait colours our view of everything else. Attractive or confident people are often judged as smarter or kinder, without evidence.

P.title: ps-social.c5.text
Psychology: We easily split the world into "us" and "them", even based on trivial things like a coin toss, and then favour our own group. Sports rivalries show it every weekend.

P.title: ps-social.c6.text
Psychology: Holding two clashing beliefs feels uncomfortable, so we change one. A smoker who knows smoking kills may tell themselves "my grandad smoked and lived to 90".

P.title: ps-social.c7.text
Psychology: We feel obliged to return favours. A free sample, a small gift or a waiter's mint makes people more likely to buy or tip.

P.title: ps-social.c8.text
Psychology: We think others notice our mistakes and appearance far more than they do. In one study, students wearing an embarrassing T-shirt guessed half the room noticed; far fewer did.

P.title: ps-social.c8.viz.unit
Psychology: % of people who noticed the shirt

P.title: ps-social.c9.text
Psychology: Social psychology isn't just about manipulation. Hotels that said "most guests reuse their towels" got more towel reuse than those that appealed to the environment.

P.title: ps-social.c9.viz.r.items.0
Psychology: Most guests in this room reuse towels

P.title: ps-emotions.summary
Psychology: What feelings are for, and what science says about happiness.

P.title: ps-emotions.q0.q
Psychology: What did the long Harvard study find best predicts a happy old age?

P.title: ps-emotions.q1.q
Psychology: Getting used to a new car and feeling the same as before is the…

P.title: ps-emotions.c0.text
Psychology: Paul Ekman found six emotions with facial expressions recognised across cultures: happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise and disgust.

P.title: ps-emotions.c1.text
Psychology: Emotions are fast signals that prepare the body to act: fear to escape, anger to defend, disgust to avoid poison, sadness to seek support.

P.title: ps-emotions.c2.text
Psychology: In danger, the amygdala triggers adrenaline: the heart races, breathing speeds up and muscles get ready. Useful against a bear, less so before a presentation.

P.title: ps-emotions.c3.text
Psychology: Putting a feeling into words ("I'm anxious about tomorrow") reduces activity in the brain's alarm system. Psychologists call it affect labelling.

P.title: ps-emotions.c3.viz.items.0.r
Psychology: I feel anxious about the meeting

P.title: ps-emotions.c4.text
Psychology: After a raise, a new car or even a lottery win, happiness tends to drift back to its usual level. We quickly adapt to good things, and fairly well to many bad ones.

P.title: ps-emotions.c5.text
Psychology: Harvard's long-running study of adult development, started in 1938, found one strong predictor of health and happiness in old age: warm, close relationships.

P.title: ps-emotions.c6.text
Psychology: Writing down three good things each day, or thanking someone in a letter, reliably boosts mood in studies. It trains attention to notice what's going well.

P.title: ps-emotions.c7.text
Psychology: Regular exercise works on mood about as well as some treatments for mild low mood, and it improves sleep and focus. Even a 10-minute walk helps.

P.title: ps-emotions.c8.text
Psychology: Carol Dweck's idea: believing abilities can be developed, rather than fixed, helps people keep going after setbacks. "I can't do this yet" beats "I'm not good at this".

P.title: ps-emotions.c8.viz.items.0.r
Psychology: I'm not good at maths yet

P.title: ps-emotions.c9.text
Psychology: When stress spikes: breathe out longer than you breathe in (in for 4, out for 6) for a minute, name the feeling, then pick one small next step. Long exhales calm the nervous system.

P.title: ps-decisions.summary
Psychology: How choices go wrong, and how to fix them.

P.title: ps-decisions.q0.q
Psychology: Opt-out organ donation systems work because of…

P.title: ps-decisions.q1.o1
Psychology: Imagining a plan failed and asking why

P.title: ps-decisions.q2.q
Psychology: Who tend to be happier with their choices?

P.title: ps-decisions.c0.text
Psychology: Each decision draws on limited mental energy. After many choices, people default to the easiest option. Steve Jobs and Barack Obama limited their wardrobe choices for this reason.

P.title: ps-decisions.c1.text
Psychology: More options can make us less happy. In a famous study, shoppers offered 6 jams were far more likely to buy than those offered 24, though later studies show the effect varies.

P.title: ps-decisions.c2.text
Psychology: Maximisers search for the best possible option; satisficers pick the first that's good enough. Satisficers tend to be happier with their choices.

P.title: ps-decisions.c3.text
Psychology: People tend to stick with the default option. Countries where organ donation is opt-out have much higher registration rates than opt-in ones.

P.title: ps-decisions.c4.text
Psychology: Before a big decision, imagine it's a year later and the plan failed. Ask "why?" This surfaces risks that optimism hides.

P.title: ps-decisions.c5.text
Psychology: Ask how you'll feel about a choice in 10 minutes, 10 months and 10 years. It balances short-term emotion with long-term goals.

P.title: ps-decisions.c6.text
Psychology: Amazon's Jeff Bezos split decisions into one-way doors (hard to undo, decide carefully) and two-way doors (easy to reverse, decide fast).

P.title: ps-decisions.c7.text
Psychology: People are often 90% sure of answers that are right only about 70% of the time. Asking for ranges and base rates helps calibrate.

P.title: ps-decisions.c8.text
Psychology: Intuition works well where you have lots of experience with fast feedback, like a firefighter or chess master. In new or noisy situations, analysis is safer.

P.title: ps-decisions.c9.text
Psychology: List options, choose a few criteria, weight them, score each option and add up. Then check: does the winner feel wrong? Ask why.

P.title: ps-persuasion.summary
Psychology: How minds are changed, for better or worse.

P.title: ps-persuasion.q0.q
Psychology: Asking for a small favour before a big one is called…

P.title: ps-persuasion.q1.q
Psychology: Only 2 rooms left! uses which principle?

P.title: ps-persuasion.c0.text
Psychology: Psychologist Robert Cialdini identified key levers of influence: reciprocity, commitment, social proof, authority, liking, scarcity and unity.

P.title: ps-persuasion.c1.text
Psychology: Things seem more valuable when rare or running out. "Only 2 rooms left!" and countdown timers push quick decisions.

P.title: ps-persuasion.c2.text
Psychology: We defer to experts and symbols of authority: uniforms, titles and white coats. Adverts use actors dressed as doctors for this reason.

P.title: ps-persuasion.c3.text
Psychology: Agreeing to a small request makes people more likely to agree to a bigger one later, to stay consistent with themselves.

P.title: ps-persuasion.c4.text
Psychology: Ask for something big first; after a refusal, a smaller request seems reasonable and people feel they should concede too.

P.title: ps-persuasion.c5.text
Psychology: We say yes to people we like: those similar to us, who compliment us or who we cooperate with. Salespeople look for common ground.

P.title: ps-persuasion.c6.text
Psychology: A single story of one child moves people to give more than statistics about millions. Our brains are wired for narratives.

P.title: ps-persuasion.c7.text
Psychology: Facts alone rarely change deep beliefs. Listening, asking questions and finding shared values work better than arguing.

P.title: ps-persuasion.c8.text
Psychology: Websites use tricks like hidden costs, confusing cancel buttons and pre-ticked boxes to steer choices. The EU now restricts many of them.

P.title: ps-persuasion.c9.text
Psychology: Next time you shop online, look for scarcity ("3 left"), social proof ("bestseller"), anchoring ("was €99") and urgency ("ends tonight").

P.title: ps-development.q0.q
Psychology: Around what age do children pass the Sally–Anne test?

P.title: ps-development.q1.q
Psychology: What does Vygotsky's "zone of proximal development" describe?

P.title: ps-development.q1.o1
Psychology: What they can do with help

P.title: ps-development.c0.text
Psychology: Jean Piaget proposed that children think in qualitatively different ways as they grow, passing through four stages.

P.title: ps-development.c1.text
Psychology: Young babies act as if hidden objects stop existing. Around 8 months they start to search for them: peek-a-boo becomes thrilling.

P.title: ps-development.c2.text
Psychology: Pour water from a short wide glass into a tall thin one and young children say there's now more. By about 7, they understand the amount stays the same.

P.title: ps-development.c3.text
Psychology: Around age 4, children grasp that others can have different beliefs. In the Sally–Anne test, they realise Sally will look where she left her ball, not where it was moved.

P.title: ps-development.c4.text
Psychology: Babies form a strong bond with caregivers. A secure attachment, built on responsive care, gives children a safe base to explore from.

P.title: ps-development.c5.text
Psychology: Toddlers go from a few words at 12 months to hundreds by age 2, and from around 18 months, often learn several new words a day.

P.title: ps-development.c6.text
Psychology: Play builds language, problem-solving, social skills and self-control. Pretend play lets children practise roles and emotions.

P.title: ps-development.c7.text
Psychology: Lev Vygotsky argued children learn best just beyond what they can do alone, with help: the "zone of proximal development".

P.title: ps-development.c7.viz.items.1
Psychology: Zone of proximal development: with help

P.title: ps-development.c8.text
Psychology: Praising effort ("you worked hard") rather than talent ("you're so clever") helps children persist after setbacks, according to Carol Dweck's research.

P.title: ps-development.c8.viz.items.0.r
Psychology: You worked really hard on that!

P.title: ps-development.c9.text
Psychology: Teenagers are especially sensitive to peers and rewards, and take more risks with friends watching. It's normal brain development, not a flaw.

P.title: ps-personality.q0.q
Psychology: What does the C in OCEAN stand for?

P.title: ps-personality.q1.o1
Psychology: No, introversion is about where you get energy

P.title: ps-personality.c0.text
Psychology: Most psychologists describe personality with five broad traits, remembered as OCEAN. Each is a spectrum, not a box.

P.title: ps-personality.c1.text
Psychology: Most people are near the middle on most traits. Popular tests that sort people into types, like the Myers–Briggs, have weak scientific support.

P.title: ps-personality.c2.text
Psychology: Extraverts gain energy from social activity; introverts recharge alone. Introversion isn't shyness, which is fear of judgement.

P.title: ps-personality.c3.text
Psychology: Conscientiousness, being organised, reliable and persistent, is one of the best personality predictors of success at work and school, and even longevity.

P.title: ps-personality.c4.text
Psychology: Twin studies suggest roughly 40–50% of personality differences are linked to genes. The rest comes from life experiences, including many that are unique to each person.

P.title: ps-personality.c5.text
Psychology: Personality isn't fixed. On average, people become more conscientious, agreeable and emotionally stable from their 20s onwards, sometimes called the maturity principle.

P.title: ps-personality.c6.text
Psychology: People act differently in different situations: quiet at work, loud with friends. Behaviour is personality plus context.

P.title: ps-personality.c7.text
Psychology: You have a lot of unused potential feels personal but fits almost everyone. Horoscopes and fake personality tests rely on these.

P.title: ps-personality.c8.text
Psychology: Psychologists study three socially aversive traits together: narcissism, Machiavellianism (manipulation) and psychopathy (callousness).

P.title: ps-personality.c9.text
Psychology: If you're low in conscientiousness, use systems: calendars, checklists, automatic savings. Design around your personality rather than fighting it.

P.title: ps-learning.q1.q
Psychology: Is the "learning styles" idea supported by evidence?

P.title: ps-learning.q1.x
Psychology: Match the format to the material instead.

P.title: ps-learning.c0.text
Psychology: Ivan Pavlov noticed dogs salivated at the sound that signalled food was coming. A neutral cue can trigger a response after being paired with something meaningful.

P.title: ps-learning.c1.text
Psychology: B.F. Skinner showed that behaviours followed by rewards become more frequent; those followed by unpleasant results become less frequent.

P.title: ps-learning.c2.text
Psychology: Rewards that come unpredictably create the most persistent behaviour. Slot machines and social media feeds use this principle.

P.title: ps-learning.c3.text
Psychology: Albert Bandura's Bobo doll study showed children copy aggressive behaviour they watch adults perform. We learn a lot by observation.

P.title: ps-learning.c4.text
Psychology: Experts improve through focused practice on weaknesses, with feedback, not just hours of repetition. The "10,000-hour rule" is a simplification.

P.title: ps-learning.c5.text
Psychology: Mixing different types of problems in one session, rather than practising one type at a time, feels harder but leads to better long-term learning.

P.title: ps-learning.c6.text
Psychology: Some struggle helps learning: testing yourself, spacing practice and explaining ideas feel slower but make memories stronger.

P.title: ps-learning.c7.text
Psychology: The idea that people learn best in their preferred "style" (visual, auditory, kinaesthetic) isn't supported by evidence. Matching content to the subject works better.

P.title: ps-learning.c7.viz.items.0.r
Psychology: Use the best format for the material

P.title: ps-learning.c8.text
Psychology: To learn something, explain it in simple words as if to a child. Where you get stuck shows the gaps in your understanding.

P.title: ps-learning.c9.text
Psychology: Combine spaced flashcards, speaking with real people early, listening daily and accepting mistakes. Ten minutes a day beats an hour on Sundays.

P.title: ps-attention.summary
Psychology: Why concentration is hard, and how to get it back.

P.title: ps-attention.q0.q
Psychology: What did the invisible gorilla study show?

P.title: ps-attention.q0.o1
Psychology: We can miss obvious things when focused

P.title: ps-attention.q1.q
Psychology: What really happens when we "multitask" on hard tasks?

P.title: ps-attention.q2.q
Psychology: How does the Pomodoro technique work?

P.title: ps-attention.q2.o1
Psychology: 25 minutes of focus, 5 minutes of break

P.title: ps-attention.c0.text
Psychology: Attention is like a spotlight: we can only focus on a little at once. Everything else is filtered out, often without us noticing.

P.title: ps-attention.c1.text
Psychology: In a famous 1999 experiment, people counting basketball passes often failed to notice a person in a gorilla suit walking through the scene. It's called inattentional blindness.

P.title: ps-attention.c2.text
Psychology: In a noisy room, you can focus on one conversation, yet you'll still notice if someone across the room says your name.

P.title: ps-attention.c3.text
Psychology: The brain doesn't truly multitask on demanding tasks; it switches between them, and every switch costs time and accuracy.

P.title: ps-attention.c4.text
Psychology: After an interruption, it can take many minutes to get fully back into deep work. Studies of office workers found an average of over 20 minutes.

P.title: ps-attention.c5.text
Psychology: Simply having your phone on the desk, even switched off, has been linked to slightly lower performance on demanding tasks in some studies. Out of sight helps.

P.title: ps-attention.c6.text
Psychology: The claim that humans have "shorter attention spans than goldfish" has no scientific basis. What changes is how often we choose to switch.

P.title: ps-attention.c6.viz.items.0.r
Psychology: No real evidence, it's switching habits

P.title: ps-attention.c7.text
Psychology: Deep, satisfying work requires sustained attention. Blocking time for single tasks is one of the simplest productivity improvements.

P.title: ps-attention.c8.text
Psychology: Work for 25 minutes on one task, then take a 5-minute break. After four rounds, take a longer break. It makes starting easier.

P.title: ps-attention.c9.text
Psychology: Time in nature restores tired attention more than city streets do, according to attention restoration research. A walk in a park before studying helps.

P.title: ps-stress.q0.q
Psychology: What happens when we avoid what we fear?

P.title: ps-stress.q1.q
Psychology: Expecting the worst possible outcome is called…

P.title: ps-stress.c0.text
Psychology: Stress is the body's response to demands. Short-term, it helps us rise to challenges. The trouble comes when it's intense and never ends.

P.title: ps-stress.c1.text
Psychology: Anxiety is worry about what might happen. It's a normal emotion, but when it's intense, constant and stops you living normally, it may be a disorder worth getting help for.

P.title: ps-stress.c2.text
Psychology: Avoiding what we fear brings quick relief but makes the fear stronger next time. Gradually facing it, called exposure, shrinks it.

P.title: ps-stress.c3.text
Psychology: Cognitive behavioural therapy identifies thinking patterns like catastrophising ("this will be a disaster") and mind-reading ("they think I'm stupid").

P.title: ps-stress.c4.text
Psychology: CBT teaches you to question automatic thoughts: what's the evidence? What would I tell a friend? What's a more balanced view?

P.title: ps-stress.c4.viz.items.0.r
Psychology: I'm prepared, and if it goes badly, I can retake it

P.title: ps-stress.c5.text
Psychology: Resilience is bouncing back from adversity. It's common, not rare, and can be strengthened through relationships, purpose and healthy habits.

P.title: ps-stress.c6.text
Psychology: Many people report positive changes after hardship: closer relationships, new priorities and a greater appreciation of life. Growth can coexist with pain.

P.title: ps-stress.c7.text
Psychology: Set aside 15 minutes a day to worry deliberately. When worries pop up at other times, note them and postpone them. Many feel smaller later.

P.title: ps-stress.c8.text
Psychology: Talking to someone you trust lowers stress hormones and helps you see problems more clearly. Isolation magnifies worries.

P.title: ps-stress.c9.text
Psychology: If anxiety or low mood lasts weeks, disrupts sleep, work or relationships, talking to a doctor or psychologist is a sign of strength, not weakness. Effective treatments exist.

P.title: ps-relationships.q0.q
Psychology: What ratio of positive to negative interactions did Gottman find in stable couples?

P.title: ps-relationships.q1.q
Psychology: Which of Gottman's "four horsemen" is most toxic?

P.title: ps-relationships.c0.text
Psychology: Humans are social animals. Loneliness raises health risks about as much as smoking, according to some major reviews.

P.title: ps-relationships.c1.text
Psychology: Early bonds shape how adults approach relationships: secure (comfortable with closeness), anxious (fears abandonment) or avoidant (uneasy with closeness).

P.title: ps-relationships.c2.text
Psychology: John Gottman found that stable couples have about five positive interactions for every negative one during conflict.

P.title: ps-relationships.c3.text
Psychology: Gottman identified four communication patterns that predict breakups: criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling. Contempt is the most toxic.

P.title: ps-relationships.c4.text
Psychology: Small moments matter: when your partner says "look at that bird", responding with interest builds connection. Couples who stayed together turned towards each other much more often.

P.title: ps-relationships.c5.text
Psychology: We tend to befriend people we see often: neighbours, classmates, colleagues. Repeated exposure breeds liking.

P.title: ps-relationships.c6.text
Psychology: Anthropologist Robin Dunbar suggested humans can maintain about 150 stable relationships, with smaller inner circles of about 5 and 15.

P.title: ps-relationships.c7.text
Psychology: Research suggests it takes roughly 50 hours together to go from acquaintance to casual friend and about 200 hours to become close friends.

P.title: ps-relationships.c8.text
Psychology: Listen to understand, not to reply. Reflect back what you heard, ask questions and resist jumping in with advice.

P.title: ps-relationships.c9.text
Psychology: Successful couples aren't those who never fight but those who repair: a joke, an apology, a touch. Repair attempts calm conflict before it escalates.

P.title: ps-perception.summary
Psychology: Your brain builds what you see.

P.title: ps-perception.q0.q
Psychology: Why don't we notice our blind spot?

P.title: ps-perception.q0.o1
Psychology: The brain fills in the gap

P.title: ps-perception.q0.o2
Psychology: We have two blind spots that cancel out

P.title: ps-perception.q1.o1
Psychology: What we see changes what we hear

P.title: ps-perception.c0.text
Psychology: Perception isn't a camera feed. The brain constantly predicts what's out there and uses the senses to correct its guesses.

P.title: ps-perception.c1.text
Psychology: Each eye has a blind spot where the optic nerve leaves the retina. You don't notice it because the brain fills in the gap.

P.title: ps-perception.c2.text
Psychology: In the Müller-Lyer illusion, two equal lines look different because of the arrows at their ends. The brain interprets them like corners in 3D.

P.title: ps-perception.c3.text
Psychology: In 2015, a photo of a dress divided the internet: blue and black or white and gold? People's brains made different assumptions about the lighting.

P.title: ps-perception.c4.text
Psychology: We see faces in clouds, plugs and car fronts. This tendency, pareidolia, comes from a brain tuned to detect faces fast.

P.title: ps-perception.c5.text
Psychology: If you watch lips saying "ga" while hearing "ba", you may hear "da". What we see changes what we hear.

P.title: ps-perception.c6.text
Psychology: People often miss big changes in a scene if they happen during a blink or cut. In one study, many didn't notice when the person they were talking to was swapped.

P.title: ps-perception.c7.text
Psychology: Expectations shape perception. "Bread" and "B13" look the same in the middle depending on context: letters or numbers.

P.title: ps-perception.c8.text
Psychology: Wine students in a 2001 study described a white wine dyed red using red-wine words. Labels, prices and colours change how food tastes.

P.title: ps-perception.c9.text
Psychology: Time feels slower when frightened and faster when absorbed. Holidays feel long in memory because of all the new experiences.

P.title: ps-creativity.q1.q
Psychology: What did the Stanford walking study find?

P.title: ps-creativity.c0.text
Psychology: Psychologists define creativity as producing ideas that are both novel and useful. Both parts matter: random isn't creative.

P.title: ps-creativity.c1.text
Psychology: Creativity needs two modes: divergent thinking generates many ideas; convergent thinking picks and refines the best.

P.title: ps-creativity.c2.text
Psychology: Prolific creators produce more hits and more flops. Picasso made tens of thousands of works. Generating many ideas makes good ones more likely.

P.title: ps-creativity.c3.text
Psychology: Stepping away from a problem often helps. Ideas can surface in the shower or on a walk, after the mind has worked on it in the background.

P.title: ps-creativity.c4.text
Psychology: Stanford researchers found people produced more creative ideas while walking than sitting. Many famous thinkers took daily walks.

P.title: ps-creativity.c5.text
Psychology: Limits can spark creativity: Dr Seuss wrote *Green Eggs and Ham* using only 50 different words, on a bet.

P.title: ps-creativity.c6.text
Psychology: Many innovations combine existing ideas in new ways: Gutenberg combined a wine press with movable type. Diverse experiences give more to combine.

P.title: ps-creativity.c7.text
Psychology: Brainstorming in groups often produces fewer ideas than individuals working alone, because people hold back. Write ideas silently first, then share.

P.title: ps-creativity.c8.text
Psychology: A positive, relaxed mood broadens thinking and helps generate ideas; a slightly critical mood helps evaluate them.

P.title: ps-creativity.c9.text
Psychology: Draw 30 circles and in three minutes turn as many as possible into objects: a clock, a ball, a face. Most people stop judging and get faster as they go.

P.title: ps-experiments.summary
Psychology: Studies that changed how we see ourselves.

P.title: ps-experiments.q0.q
Psychology: What did Harlow's monkey studies show?

P.title: ps-experiments.q0.x
Psychology: They clung to the cloth mother.

P.title: ps-experiments.q1.q
Psychology: Why is the Stanford prison experiment questioned today?

P.title: ps-experiments.q1.o1
Psychology: Guards were coached and methods were weak

P.title: ps-experiments.q2.q
Psychology: Roughly what share of 100 psychology studies replicated in 2015?

P.title: ps-experiments.c0.text
Psychology: In 1971, students played guards and prisoners; it was stopped after six days as guards became abusive. Later reviews found guards were coached, so its conclusions are now heavily questioned.

P.title: ps-experiments.c1.text
Psychology: The 1970s study suggested children who waited for a second treat did better later in life. A larger 2018 replication found the link much weaker once family background was considered.

P.title: ps-experiments.c2.text
Psychology: In 1920, John Watson conditioned a baby to fear a white rat by pairing it with loud noises. It showed fears can be learnt, and would never pass ethics review today.

P.title: ps-experiments.c3.text
Psychology: In the 1950s, Harry Harlow found baby monkeys preferred a soft cloth "mother" over a wire one that gave milk. Comfort and touch matter, not just food.

P.title: ps-experiments.c4.text
Psychology: In 1954, Muzafer Sherif split boys at a summer camp into two groups. Competition bred hostility; shared goals, like fixing the water supply together, reduced it.

P.title: ps-experiments.c5.text
Psychology: Teachers told that certain random pupils would "bloom" treated them differently, and those pupils' scores rose. Expectations can shape outcomes.

P.title: ps-experiments.c6.text
Psychology: Seminary students hurrying to give a talk, even one about the Good Samaritan, often walked past a man in distress. Time pressure mattered more than values.

P.title: ps-experiments.c7.text
Psychology: In 2015, a project tried to repeat 100 psychology studies and successfully replicated only about 36–40%. Science improved its methods as a result.

P.title: ps-experiments.c8.text
Psychology: Psychology now encourages larger samples, registering plans before collecting data and sharing data openly, making findings more trustworthy.

P.title: ps-experiments.c9.text
Psychology: After controversial experiments, research ethics boards now require informed consent, the right to withdraw, minimal harm and debriefing.

P.title: ps-communication.q0.o1
Psychology: I feel ignored when plans change last minute

P.title: ps-communication.q1.q
Psychology: In negotiation, what should you focus on?

P.title: ps-communication.c0.text
Psychology: Tone, facial expression and posture carry a lot of meaning, especially for feelings. The often-quoted "93% non-verbal" figure is a misreading of a narrow study.

P.title: ps-communication.c0.viz.items.0.r
Psychology: Non-verbal cues matter a lot, but words matter too

P.title: ps-communication.c1.text
Psychology: You never listen! triggers defence. "I feel unheard when I'm interrupted" describes your experience and invites a solution.

P.title: ps-communication.c1.viz.items.0.r
Psychology: I feel unheard when I'm interrupted

P.title: ps-communication.c2.text
Psychology: Marshall Rosenberg's method has four steps: observe without judging, name the feeling, state the need, and make a clear request.

P.title: ps-communication.c3.text
Psychology: Most people listen while preparing their reply. Summarising what you heard ("so you're saying…") shows understanding and reduces conflict.

P.title: ps-communication.c4.text
Psychology: Once you know something, it's hard to imagine not knowing it. Experts often explain too fast and skip steps.

P.title: ps-communication.c5.text
Psychology: Specific, timely, behaviour-focused feedback works best. "In the meeting, you interrupted Ana twice" is more useful than "you're rude".

P.title: ps-communication.c5.viz.items.0.r
Psychology: In the meeting you interrupted Ana twice

P.title: ps-communication.c6.text
Psychology: When criticised, pause before reacting, ask questions to understand, thank the person and decide later what to act on.

P.title: ps-communication.c7.text
Psychology: In heated moments, lowering your voice, slowing down, acknowledging feelings and taking a break if needed calms things down.

P.title: ps-communication.c8.text
Psychology: Focus on interests, not positions. Two people fighting over an orange may want different parts: one the juice, one the peel for a cake.

P.title: ps-communication.c9.text
Psychology: A clear, kind "no" respects both people: "Thanks for thinking of me. I can't take this on right now, but I could help next month."

P.title: ps-communication.c9.viz.steps.3
Psychology: Offer an alternative if you want

P.title: ps-work.q0.q
Psychology: What did Google find most important for team success?

P.title: ps-work.q1.q
Psychology: Why do people underestimate how long tasks will take?

P.title: ps-work.c0.text
Psychology: Google's Project Aristotle found that the top factor in effective teams was psychological safety: people feel safe to take risks and admit mistakes.

P.title: ps-work.c1.text
Psychology: For creative work, Daniel Pink argues money matters up to a point, then autonomy, mastery and purpose drive motivation.

P.title: ps-work.c2.text
Psychology: The WHO describes burnout as an occupational phenomenon from chronic workplace stress, with exhaustion, cynicism and reduced effectiveness.

P.title: ps-work.c3.text
Psychology: People may change their behaviour simply because they know they're being observed. The original 1920s factory studies are debated, but the idea endures.

P.title: ps-work.c4.text
Psychology: In groups, individuals often put in less effort than alone, because responsibility is shared. Clear individual roles reduce it.

P.title: ps-work.c5.text
Psychology: Cohesive groups can suppress dissent to keep harmony, leading to bad decisions. Assigning a "devil's advocate" helps.

P.title: ps-work.c6.text
Psychology: We underestimate how long tasks will take, even when we know past projects ran late. Use past similar projects to estimate instead.

P.title: ps-work.c7.text
Psychology: Many meetings are too long and too large. Clear agendas, fewer people and ending with decisions and owners make them work.

P.title: ps-work.c8.text
Psychology: Being recognised for good work is a strong motivator, often more than small bonuses. Specific and sincere thanks matter most.

P.title: ps-work.c8.viz.items.0.r
Psychology: Your analysis saved us two weeks, thank you

P.title: ps-work.c9.text
Psychology: Cal Newport argues that the ability to focus without distraction on demanding tasks is increasingly rare and valuable. Protect blocks of time for it.

P.title: ps-digital.summary
Psychology: Screens, feeds and the attention economy.

P.title: ps-digital.q0.q
Psychology: Why do feeds feel so gripping?

P.title: ps-digital.q1.o1
Psychology: Remembering less when info is easy to find

P.title: ps-digital.c0.text
Psychology: Many free apps earn money from advertising, so they're designed to capture as much of your attention as possible.

P.title: ps-digital.c0.viz.steps.3
Psychology: More features to keep you hooked

P.title: ps-digital.c1.text
Psychology: Endless feeds remove natural stopping points. Without a "bottom", people tend to keep going much longer than they intend.

P.title: ps-digital.c2.text
Psychology: Likes, messages and new posts arrive unpredictably, like a slot machine. That unpredictability keeps us checking.

P.title: ps-digital.c3.text
Psychology: Feeds show others' highlights. Comparing your everyday life with their best moments can lower mood and self-esteem.

P.title: ps-digital.c4.text
Psychology: Fear of missing out drives compulsive checking. Turning off non-essential notifications reduces it more than willpower does.

P.title: ps-digital.c5.text
Psychology: Using screens late at night delays sleep, mostly because content keeps us engaged, and partly through light. Charging the phone outside the bedroom helps.

P.title: ps-digital.c6.text
Psychology: Algorithms show content similar to what we already engage with. Over time, we can see less of other viewpoints.

P.title: ps-digital.c7.text
Psychology: If we know information is saved, we put less effort into remembering it. It's called the "Google effect".

P.title: ps-digital.c8.text
Psychology: Technology also connects friends, teaches skills and supports health. How and why you use it matters more than total screen time.

P.title: ps-digital.c9.text
Psychology: Turn off all non-human notifications, move social apps off the home screen, use grayscale at night and set app timers.

P.title: ps-digital.c9.viz.items.1
Psychology: Social apps off the home screen

P.title: ps-intelligence.summary
Psychology: What it is, and what it isn't.

P.title: ps-intelligence.q0.q
Psychology: What's the average IQ score by design?

P.title: ps-intelligence.q1.q
Psychology: Which kind of intelligence keeps growing into old age?

P.title: ps-intelligence.c0.text
Psychology: Intelligence broadly means the ability to learn, reason, solve problems and adapt. Psychologists still debate exactly how to define it.

P.title: ps-intelligence.c1.text
Psychology: IQ tests measure reasoning, memory, vocabulary and processing speed. Scores are scaled so the average is 100, with most people between 85 and 115.

P.title: ps-intelligence.c2.text
Psychology: People who do well on one kind of mental test tend to do well on others. Psychologists call this shared factor "g", general intelligence.

P.title: ps-intelligence.c3.text
Psychology: Howard Gardner proposed separate intelligences, like musical, bodily and interpersonal. It's popular in schools but has limited scientific support.

P.title: ps-intelligence.c3.viz.r.items.0
Psychology: a general factor plus specific abilities

P.title: ps-intelligence.c4.text
Psychology: Average IQ scores rose about 3 points per decade during the 20th century, likely due to better nutrition, schooling and more abstract thinking in daily life.

P.title: ps-intelligence.c5.text
Psychology: Fluid intelligence, solving new problems, peaks in early adulthood. Crystallised intelligence, knowledge and vocabulary, keeps growing into old age.

P.title: ps-intelligence.c6.text
Psychology: Emotional intelligence is the ability to recognise, understand and manage emotions in yourself and others. It matters for relationships and leadership.

P.title: ps-intelligence.c7.text
Psychology: Brain-training games mostly improve the games themselves. Education, reading, learning new skills and good sleep have broader benefits.

P.title: ps-intelligence.c8.text
Psychology: Success also depends on persistence, curiosity, health, relationships and opportunity. IQ predicts some outcomes but leaves much unexplained.

P.title: ps-intelligence.c9.text
Psychology: Wisdom, combining knowledge with judgement, humility and care for others, isn't the same as intelligence. Smart people can still make foolish choices.

P.title: ps-intelligence.c9.viz.r.items.0
Psychology: choosing which problems to solve and how
